title: Schema validation for API boundaries
description: Learn how schema validation libraries bridge the gap between backend types and frontend TypeScript code.

data.text: APIs are contracts between the server and the browser. The server promises a shape, and the browser promises to use it correctly. But promises are not enough. Schema validation gives you a single source of truth that lives in both TypeScript types and runtime checks.

A schema describes the shape of your data. Instead of writing an interface by hand and hoping the JSON matches, you describe the data once and derive both the type and the runtime check from it. If the server returns something different, you find out immediately.

data.content: Defining and inferring a type from a schema

data.text: The biggest benefit of schema validation is a single definition that both the backend and frontend understand. If you generate schemas from your database or API layer, the frontend automatically stays in sync when the backend changes.

items: Generate schemas from your database using Prisma, Drizzle, or tRPC
Share schema packages between server and client
Use schema inference to avoid duplicated interfaces
Fail fast with clear error messages when data is wrong

data.text: Schema validation is not only for APIs. Forms are another major boundary. User input is untrusted by definition, so validating it against a schema before submission prevents corrupt data from ever reaching your server.

data.title: Form Schema and Validation
data.content: Validating form input with a schema

data.title: Validate at Every Boundary
data.text: API responses, form submissions, cookies, localStorage, and WebSocket messages are all external inputs. Each one should be validated with a schema before it is trusted by your application.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Schemas describe data shape in one place
Infer TypeScript types from schemas instead of duplicating them
Use schemas for API responses, forms, and shared packages
Validation libraries give clear errors when data is wrong
data.takeaway: Schema validation turns vague runtime errors into predictable, typed data flows across your entire stack.
